newsitem.title: HUNGARY: INTERVIEW - HUNGARY RADIO, TV MKT SEEN CARVED UP-ORTT.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - HUNGARY RADIO, TV MKT SEEN CARVED UP-ORTT.

text.p: The man in charge of reshaping Hungary's electronic media said bidders in TV and radio tenders can rest assured no new frequencies will be added later on.

"That is an easy promise to make since there are no other TV frequencies available and the same goes for radio, too," Mihaly Revesz, head of national radio and television body ORTT, told Reuters in a recent interview.
Revesz, a strong personality at the helm of the all-party ORTT board, has been portrayed by the Hungarian media as seeking to turn the media into a "Revesz empire".

Revesz denied that, saying apparent delays in privatisation that began when a media law was passed in December 1995 are an inevitable result of the complications involved and did not arise him trying to create a power base.
"We could have announced the tenders earlier, based on insufficient information but there would have been no way for the TV stations to go on the air," he said.
"The frequency maps were drawn up (last) October, the broadcasting and frequency fees were set in April and the broadcasting infrastructure will be in place in September".
Three bidders are in the race for 10-year concessions for two commercial TV channels, on offer for eight billion forints plus 25 percent VAT each, three years payable in advance.

The Swedish-Hungarian consortium of SBS-MTM submitted a bid for one channel, a consortium of CLT-Bertelsmann for the other while U.S.-based Central European Media Enterprises (CME) is in the race for both.
Only consortia were allowed to bid, no single company is allowed to have more than a 49 percent stake and Hungarians have to hold a minimum of 26 percent.
Under Hungary's media law, the winners must go on air three months after the concession contracts have been signed.
After the first round the ORTT announced that CME was ahead of CLT in the race for Channel Two and that MTM was ahead of CME in the competition for the other commercial channel.
"This was partly to encourage higher bids...but the differences are not very significant and the situation can still be turned around," he said.
A final decision is expected by the end of June. Revesz said he hopes new stations can go on the air on September 1.
He also said that when this happens, he wants ORTT to clamp down on violations of advertising regulations by the state-owned broadcasting company MTV.
ORTT officials say MTV shows product brands in its programmes, which they regard as hidden advertising.

"MTV had been exempted from these regulations by a budget bill passed (by parliament) with a 94 percent majority," Revesz said. "We will be obliged by contract to ensure (commercial television stations) that the other side does not curtail them by illegal means."
Some potential bidders have criticised the radio tenders, to be announced soon, for setting an asking price which they deem too high at three billion forints apiece for seven years.
Potential bidders have said the terms could jeopardise profitability and were excessive compared with Poland's asking price of an equivalent of 90 million forints.
Revesz acknowledged the asking price was high, but said it would still allow for a good profit.

"With annual advertising income around 1.2 billion to 1.3 billion forints, (proportional) concession fee of 450 million and production costs at around 300 million, this still leaves a 400 million forints profit per year," Revesz said.
"This amounts to a 100 percent return of a three billion forints investment in seven years".
He said, however, that European bidders' expectations were more realistic than those of their U.S. counterparts.
"Europeans know that one cannot expect a 200 percent profit," Revesz said. "But despite their concern, I think they will submit bids".

UK's DMG Radio, part of the Daily Mail and General Trust Plc; a French-German consortium of Europe Development International (EDI) and the Marquardt group, U.S.'s Emmis International and Clear Channel International have signalled their interest in the radio tenders.
Revesz said the radio tenders allow more programming freedom than the TV tenders.
"We might consider easing some of the tight rules in the TV tenders when we sign the concession contracts," he added.
